questions.q: Per the lesson, what does 'it depends' mean when choosing an operating model?
options: It only depends on the CEO's personal preference
The choice should be made randomly
It depends on specific, answerable questions — not vague judgment or whichever model sounds most sophisticated
There is genuinely no way to ever decide
questions.explain: The lesson frames 'it depends' as the honest answer, but backs it with a concrete five-question decision framework rather than leaving it vague.

questions.q: Which of these is one of the five questions in the lesson's decision framework?
options: How many floors does the headquarters building have?
How much cross-cutting data actually needs to be consistent across the organization?
What programming language does the IT team prefer?
What color is the company logo?
questions.explain: The five real questions cover business-unit diversity, cross-cutting data needs, maturity, sponsorship, and speed requirements.

questions.q: In the worked healthcare example, what factor pushed toward a federated model with a narrow central scope?
options: The company having no regulatory obligations at all
Three distinct business units all touching HIPAA-regulated patient data, requiring strong central consistency on that specific data
A complete absence of any executive sponsorship
All three business units being functionally identical
questions.explain: Distinct business units leaned federated, while shared HIPAA-regulated patient data created a strong case for centrally governing that specific cross-cutting data.

questions.q: Why did the worked example recommend a staged rollout rather than full federation on day one?
options: Because the company had no data at all
Because staged rollouts are always required by law
Because the organization's governance maturity was low — a fully federated model's complexity wasn't realistic yet
Because federated models are illegal for healthcare companies
questions.explain: Low current maturity (Lesson 9's concept) argued for starting narrower and expanding central scope only as the organization matures.

questions.q: What does the lesson say happens to a nominally federated model without real executive sponsorship?
options: It quietly degrades into decentralized in practice, since there's no authority to enforce the centrally-governed parts
It instantly achieves full regulatory compliance
It automatically becomes fully centralized instead
It has no effect on the model at all
questions.explain: Both federated and centralized models require real authority to enforce their centrally-governed parts — without sponsorship, that authority doesn't exist in practice.
